content: Many women prefer to avoid pharmacological or invasive methods for managing pain during labor, which has led to the growing popularity of complementary approaches. This review aimed to evaluate the current evidence on the use of relaxation techniques for pain management during labor. It is an update of a review initially published in 2011. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of mind-body relaxation techniques on maternal and neonatal well-being during and after labor. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases and clinical trial registries up to May 2017. Randomized controlled trials (including quasi-randomized and cluster trials) comparing relaxation methods with standard care, no treatment, other non-pharmacological pain management methods, or placebo were included. Two reviewers independently assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE methodology. This updated review included 19 studies involving 2,519 women, with data from 15 studies (1,731 women) contributing to the analysis. The interventions examined included relaxation, yoga, music, and mindfulness. Approximately half of the studies had a low risk of bias for random sequence generation and attrition bias, but most had a high risk of performance and detection bias, as well as unclear risks for allocation concealment, reporting bias, and other biases. The quality of evidence ranged from low to very low, and the findings should be interpreted with caution. Relaxation Techniques: Relaxation techniques, compared to usual care, were associated with a reduction in pain intensity during the latent phase of labor (measured on a 0-10 scale, with lower scores indicating less pain). One trial involving 40 women reported a mean difference (MD) of -1.25 (95% confidence interval [CI] -1.97 to -0.53). For the active phase of labor, four trials (271 women) showed high heterogeneity, and very low-quality evidence suggested no strong difference in pain intensity between groups (MD -1.08, 95% CI -2.57 to 0.41). Women receiving relaxation reported greater satisfaction with pain relief during labor (risk ratio [RR] 8.00, 95% CI 1.10 to 58.19, one trial, 40 women). However, there was no clear benefit for satisfaction with the childbirth experience (standard mean difference [SMD] -0.03, 95% CI -0.37 to 0.31, three trials, 1,176 women). Very low-quality evidence indicated no clear reduction in assisted vaginal births (average RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.20 to 1.84, four trials, 1,122 women) or cesarean section rates (average RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.26 to 2.01, four trials, 1,122 women). Outcomes related to sense of control during labor and breastfeeding were not reported. Yoga: Low-quality evidence suggested that yoga reduced pain intensity (measured on a 0-10 scale, with lower scores indicating less pain) (MD -6.12, 95% CI -11.77 to -0.47, one trial, 66 women). Yoga was associated with greater satisfaction with pain relief (MD 7.88, 95% CI 1.51 to 14.25, one trial, 66 women) and greater satisfaction with the childbirth experience (MD 6.34, 95% CI 0.26 to 12.42, one trial, 66 women, assessed using the Maternal Comfort Scale, where higher scores indicate greater comfort). Outcomes related to sense of control during labor, breastfeeding, assisted vaginal births, and cesarean sections were not reported. Music: Evidence suggested that music reduced pain intensity during the latent phase of labor (measured on a 0-10 scale, with lower scores indicating less pain) (MD -0.73, 95% CI -1.01 to -0.45, two trials, 192 women). However, very low-quality evidence indicated no clear benefit during the active phase (MD -0.51, 95% CI -1.10 to 0.07, three trials, 217 women). Very low-quality evidence suggested no clear benefit in reducing assisted vaginal births (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.08 to 2.05, one trial, 156 women) or cesarean section rates (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.70, two trials, 216 women). Outcomes related to satisfaction with pain relief, sense of control during labor, satisfaction with the childbirth experience, and breastfeeding were not reported. Audio Analgesia: One trial evaluated audio analgesia compared to control and reported no evidence of benefit in satisfaction with pain relief. Mindfulness: One trial comparing mindfulness to usual care found an increase in the sense of control during labor for the mindfulness group (measured using the Childbirth Self-Efficacy Inventory) (MD 31.30, 95% CI 1.61 to 60.99, 26 women). There was no strong evidence of differences between groups for satisfaction with childbirth, cesarean section rates, assisted vaginal delivery, or the need for pharmacological pain relief. No other outcomes were reported. Conclusions: Relaxation techniques, yoga, and music may play a role in reducing pain and increasing satisfaction with pain relief during labor, although the quality of evidence varies from very low to low. There is insufficient evidence to support the effectiveness of mindfulness and audio analgesia. Most trials did not report on the safety of these interventions. Further randomized controlled trials are needed to evaluate relaxation modalities for pain management during labor. These trials should be adequately powered and include clinically relevant outcomes, such as those described in this review.
